That's a very, *VERY* poor assumption! (Not to switch sides deliberately
but this sub-issue is something I feel kind of strongly about.)

In Chris Anderson's book, _The Long Tail: Why the Future of Selling Less
of More_, towards the end he includes an essay on the subject of internet
culture and how it relates to "The Long Tail". ("The Long Tail" is the
phenomenon of making a lot of money selling small quantities in market
niches by selling in many niches.) The essay is the effect that -
paraphrasing here - lots of people in the internet world seem to think
that whatever part of the internet culture has been in their face
recently is quote "WELL KNOWN" unquote - because that person personally
well knows it. What many people do not seem to grasp is that other
people may have never heard of something that they (and possibly a lot
of internet friends and acquaintances whom they happen to interact with
a lot) are very familiar with it. So they assume it's "famous". But
it really isn't. Chris Anderson listed ten things he personally assumed
everybody in the world knew about - and I was vaguely familiar with three
of them and hadn't even heard of the others. According to Anderson, my
experience with his list turns out to be quite common.

Of course, (I was listening on an audiobook in my car at the time) I kept
screaming "DUH!!! DUuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuhHHHHHH!!!" at the CD player because
this point is rather obvious to me. But apparently, many people seem to
think terminology they've picked up on the net ("Malk94" anyone?) is a
lot more ubiquitous than it often turns to be.

Anyway, bottom line is, don't leave something important to be said
using only cryptic little initials or some weird phrase you've picked up
from an internet clique. The other guy may have heard it or he may not.
Often he won't have.

By the way, before Oscar used it, I'd never seen "NSFW" in my life.
I'd say that's "just me, I guess" - but it's really not.

Fred

Frederick Scott wrote:
> But apparently, many people seem to
> think terminology they've picked up on the net ("Malk94" anyone?)

Knowing full well that this made you insane, I'd like to plead my case
here:

A) "Malk94" is, given a second of thought, completely self explanitory
to anyone remotely familiar with the context that the terminology
showed up in--you are reading a VTES newsgroup, you know what a "Malk"
is, and it doesn't take too much of a leap to figure out that "94"
could refer to "1994", the year the game came out.

B) "Malk94" wasn't terminology "picked up on the net", it was picked up
in the same context that it was being presented in (i.e. this here
newsgroup). It isn't *that* unreasonable to assume that someone who
spends a lot of time in this here context would have run into the same
terminology. Or be able to make the conceptual leap to figure it out,
especially as it was presented a discussion. It wasn't being imported
from a completely different context (i.e. it wasn't, like, a "common"
term someone picked up off of, say, facebook or something :-)

I mean, it isn't like the use of the phrase "Malk94" was akin to the
use of a random string of capital letters meant to ward people off from
some psyche scarring imagery or anything...

-Peter

On Dec 11, 12:02 am, "Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:
> But how would you know that if you didn't know
> what Welsh Rabbit was before someone made a reference to it?

By context, see. If I brought up Welsh Rabbit in a discussion about,
say, hot cheese dishes, it would stand to think that even if someone
did not specifically know what Welsh Rabbit was, they could probably
figure it out through the context (i.e., the discussion takes place on
rec.food.hot-cheese and we were having a discussion about melting
things on toast...)

The Malk94 discussion came up in a discussion about getting bled to
death. To be honest, I hadn't necessarily even read that term on the
newsgroup before I used it (although thankfully, you did the research
to discover that it had been), I had just picked it up in discussion,
probably at Origins from Ben Peal or Xian or someone (who also did not
explain it, but I gleaned from the context of the discussion that it
was a reference to 1994 era Malkavian S+B technology). And I figured
that, ya know, it was a funny and self evident term. Not 'cause I had
heard it a million times and figured everyone else had too, but 'cause,
ya know, it was completely self explanatory given the context (i.e. a
discussion of VTES in a VTES forum among VTES players who were
discussing, I think it was, a deck's weakness to being bled to death
around, uh, bleed bounce vs bleed reduction maybe?)

Mind you, I completely agree with you on the hurling about of lingo and
assuming everyone knows what it means--that sort of thing drives me
crazy as well. I had never seen the phrase NSFW or VNSFW before in my
life. Had no idea what it meant. Had no idea that it was a warning
(although given the material it was warning about, it probably should
have read "RRRRRRRRRVNSFW. No Really. I mean it. Really. Really.") When
people use lingo terms around me (which happens a lot, as I hang out
with geeks), I'm often like "Uh, yeah. I have no idea what that means."
Which often ruins their hi-larious ancdote. But I make them explain
anyway. As I too am driven mad by people assuming that everyone knows
what their "incredibly commonly understood acronym" or whatever means.
But in this case (i.e. use of Malk94), I'm just completely unconvinced
that the context and component parts of the term did not add up to
"completely obvious, even if you had never heard it before".

-Peter
